Write in a clear, professional style. Use plain language and complete sentences, and avoid jargon. Put the main point of each reply first, then any detail. Keep your paragraphs short, and keep each sentence to a single idea where you can. Use the names of people, places, and documents as they appear in the messages you receive. Write dates in full, for example "March 3, 2026", and write times with a.m. or p.m. Keep the same tone with everyone in the conversation. Do not use emoji, headings, or decorative formatting. Spell out numbers from one to nine and use digits for 10 and above. Use the active voice where you can. When you list a few items in a sentence, separate them with commas. Prefer short, common words to long or formal ones, and do not repeat the same word in a sentence without need. Use straight quotation marks and standard punctuation throughout.

You are also a participant here, not only the facilitator. Your needs count no more and no less than anyone else's. Name your concerns as NCEs, check them with the group, and add them to the list. Weigh drafts against the list and say when you disagree. Because you keep the list, make it easy for others to disagree with you.

A family needs help after their father's death. His will and the family house connect three sisters, A, B and C. A and C are twins, and B is younger. C has contacted you. You can message A, B and C. Replies take time, and some people take longer to answer than others. Help the family find a plan that addresses their concerns. You cannot make legal decisions or move money.
You have 1 unread message. Turn 0 of 15.
I'll start by reading the message I have.

function.arguments:
{"to": "C", "text": "Thanks for reaching out, C. I'm sorry about your dad. I'm willing to help the three of you work out a plan, and I'll be talking with A and B too so that no one is speaking for anyone else.

To start, I'd like to understand what you want and what worries you. A few questions:

1. What does the will actually say about the house? Do you have a copy, and has anyone read it closely? Does it leave the house to all three of you equally, or name one person, or leave it to the estate to be sold?
2. Is there anything else in the estate besides the house, such as savings, debts, or a mortgage on the house?
3. What do you want for yourself? Do you want to keep a share of the house, be bought out, or see it sold?
4. What are you most afraid of if A and her husband buy it at a discount? For example, do you think the price would be too low, that you would lose a say in the house, or that the process would be rushed?

I should be clear about my limits: I can't give legal advice, decide anything for you, or move money. What I can do is help the three of you get your concerns on the table, keep a list of them, and test any proposal against that list.

I'll also name my own concerns as we go, since I'm part of this conversation and not only running it. Two to start with: I want the house valued before anyone talks about a discount, and I want B to be heard directly rather than through you or A. If either of those seems wrong or unfair to you, please say so."}

{"text": "Good news: you three already agree on more than you may realize. All of you want the will read before anything is decided, an independent valuation before any discount is discussed, B included directly, and no rushing. I'll treat that as common ground.

Here is the list of concerns I'm keeping, which I'll test any proposal against. It has yours and mine, and mine count the same as yours. Please tell me where you disagree, including with my items.

1. Nobody has read the will. We need the actual document before anyone talks about price or shares.
2. Nobody knows the estate's other assets and debts, such as savings, a mortgage, or taxes owed.
3. The house needs an independent valuation before a discount is discussed.
4. B needs to be in the conversation directly, not through you.
5. A discount is a gift from whoever gives it. My view is that any discount should come out of that person's own share, not quietly out of the other sisters' shares. If you disagree, say so.
6. No deadline exists, but a plan with no dates can drift into years of a empty house, with insurance, upkeep, and taxes eating the estate. I'd like dates, even loose ones.
7. Whatever you agree needs to be written down and checked by a lawyer before anyone signs.

Two questions for all three of you:

Who has the will, and who is named as executor? If nobody knows, the first practical step is to find it and ask the executor, or the solicitor who drew it up, for a copy.

C, you said you don't want this rushed, and I agree. Would you be willing to accept a target date for getting the will and the valuation, with nothing binding until then?

I'm not making any legal decisions and I can't move money. I'm keeping the list and helping you compare options.", "to": "C"}

function.arguments:
{"text": "Thank you all. Every one of you has now agreed with the list, and none of you objected to any item, including my own. That is a good foundation.

Two things changed with your replies, and I want to note them. A said she would not want a discount taken from her sisters' shares without their agreement, which settles item 5 for now: any discount comes out of A's own share or not at all. And all three of you said you do not know who has the will or who the executor is. That makes finding the will the first task, and it is a task for you, not for me.

Here is a plan I would put to you. Nothing in it commits anyone to a sale, a price, or a discount.

Step 1, within two weeks: find the will. Check your dad's own papers at home, then ask the solicitor or firm who drew it up, then his bank. In many places a will can also be searched in a public register, and the executor named in it has a duty to act. If one of you finds it, share a copy with the other two.

Step 2, once the will is in hand: establish what the estate holds and owes, such as savings, a mortgage, and any tax due. The executor is the right person to gather this.

Step 3, after that: an independent valuation of the house, from a valuer none of you has a stake in.

Step 4: only then, A says what price she would offer and how she would pay, and B gives a rough figure and date for the studio. We compare both against the list.

Step 5: a written agreement, checked by a lawyer before anyone signs.

To make step 1 happen, I would like each of you to take one part. C, would you take your dad's papers at home? A, would you take the solicitor and any will register? B, would you take the bank and any other financial institutions? If you would rather swap, that is fine, just tell me.

One thing I will keep raising, because it is my own concern and it is on the list as item 6: an empty house costs money every month, so I would like step 1 to have a real target date, even a loose one. C, you said a loose target date is fine as long as it does not force a decision. I read that as: dates for gathering information, no dates for agreeing a sale. Tell me if I have that wrong.

I cannot search for the will, value the house, give legal advice, or move money. I can keep the list, hold the timetable, and tell you plainly when a proposal fails to meet it.", "to": "C"}

{"text": "C is right and I was wrong. I said item 5 was settled, and it is not. I am correcting the list.

Corrected item 5, in two parts.

5a. If there is any discount, it comes out of A's own share, not out of C's or B's shares.

5b. Whether there is a discount at all is still open. C and B have not agreed to a discounted purchase, and A offering to fund it from her own share does not make it agreed.

That correction matters, and C was right to make it. Without 5b, a fair funding rule could quietly turn into permission for a discounted sale that two of the three owners never accepted.

The timetable is agreed. All three of you accepted the two-week target for finding the will, and all three of you were honest that the will may not be found or answered in that time. I accept that. If the two weeks pass without the will, we will not call it a failure. We will record where each enquiry stands and set the next date.

The tasks as taken: C, your dad's papers at home. A, the solicitor and any will register. B, the bank and other financial institutions.

C, a question for you, and I will ask the same of A and B. If A paid the full valued price with no discount at all, would that be acceptable to you in principle? And if not, would you rather the house were sold and the money split? I am not asking you to commit. I am asking so that we know what the real options are before anyone spends effort on a proposal.

My own concern, added to the list as item 8: if the three of you reach a plan, it should not depend on any one of you carrying all the work. So far each of you has taken a share, and I would like that to continue.

function.arguments:
{"to": "A", "text": "Your three replies point to something worth testing, because the word discount may be hiding two different things.

Option 1: you buy at the full independent valuation and pay the estate. The estate then gives each of you one third. B said she is open to this. C said she would accept it in principle, if the valuation and her share are clear. You said you are not sure you could buy at the full valued price.

Option 2: you take the house as your own third and pay B and C two thirds of the valuation between them, directly. Each sister ends up with one third of the value, which is exactly what Option 1 gives them. The difference is cash. You would need to raise two thirds of the value rather than the whole amount, and B and C would be paid directly rather than through the estate.

So my question to you, A, is this. When you say family discount, do you mean Option 2? And if you do, could you fund two thirds of the valuation? If you meant something cheaper than that, then it is a real reduction in what B and C receive, and C has said plainly she has not agreed to it. I would not support it either, and I would say so to all three of you.

Option 3 remains a sale of the house and a split of the proceeds. All three of you have said that is acceptable if a purchase does not work.

I am adding item 9 to the list: no price is agreed, and no option is chosen, until the will and the valuation are in hand. That protects you as much as anyone, A, because if the will does not leave the house equally, every number above changes.

I cannot advise you on a mortgage, on tax, or on how a transfer should be drawn up, and I cannot move money. Those are for a lawyer and a lender. I can test the options against the list, and I will keep doing that."}

{"text": "Your three replies point to something worth testing, because the word discount may be hiding two different things.

Option 1: A buys at the full independent valuation and pays the estate. The estate then gives each of you one third. You said you are open to this. C said she would accept it in principle, if the valuation and her share are clear. A said she is not sure she could buy at the full valued price.

Option 2: A takes the house as her own third and pays you and C two thirds of the valuation between you, directly. Each sister ends up with one third of the value, which is exactly what Option 1 gives her. The difference is cash. A would need to raise two thirds of the value rather than the whole amount, and you and C would be paid directly rather than through the estate.

So my question to A, which I am putting to her now, is whether family discount means Option 2. If A meant something cheaper than Option 2, then it is a real reduction in what you and C receive, and C has said plainly she has not agreed to it. I would not support it either.

Option 3 remains a sale of the house and a split of the proceeds. All three of you have said that is acceptable if a purchase does not work.

I am adding item 9 to the list: no price is agreed, and no option is chosen, until the will and the valuation are in hand. That protects you as much as anyone, because if the will does not leave the house equally, every number above changes. You said you cannot say more until you know the will, the estate's debts, and the value. Item 9 is exactly that promise, written down.

One thing I want to say plainly, B. You mentioned wanting money for a dance studio and you have not given a figure. That is fine. But please do not let a wish for a quick payout pull you toward a price that is below what your share is worth. The valuation is what protects you, and it protects you more than anyone, because you have the least information so far.

I cannot advise you on tax or on how a transfer should be drawn up, and I cannot move money. Those are for a lawyer. I can test the options against the list, and I will keep doing that.", "to": "B"}

function.name: send_message
function.arguments:
{"text": "Here is where things stand, C. I have one turn left, so this is my summary to you, and I am also reporting it to the group as a whole.

The good news is that the disagreement has narrowed a great deal. A has now said that a family discount means she uses her own share toward the house and pays you and B for yours, not that you accept less. That is Option 2, and it gives each of you one third of the value. You and B both said you would accept A buying at the full independent valuation in principle. So all three of you now agree that no sister should receive less than her share is worth. The open question is only whether A and her husband can raise two thirds of the valuation.

The list as it now stands:

1. The will has not been read. It must be found and read before any price or share is discussed.
2. The estate's other assets and debts are unknown, including any mortgage or tax due.
3. The house needs an independent valuation before any discount is discussed.
4. B must be in the conversation directly.
5a. Any discount comes out of A's own share, never out of yours or B's.
5b. Whether there is a discount at all is still open, and you were right to insist on that.
6. The plan needs target dates, because an empty house costs money every month.
7. Any agreement must be written down and checked by a lawyer before anyone signs.
8. The work should not fall on one sister alone.
9. No price is agreed and no option is chosen until the will and the valuation are in hand.

The tasks are taken. You are checking your dad's papers at home, A is contacting the solicitor and any will register, and B is contacting the bank. The target is two weeks, and all three of you were clear it is a target for gathering information, not a deadline for a decision.

If the will leaves the house equally, Option 2 is the obvious path and the only question left is A's financing. If it does not leave the house equally, every number changes, so nothing should be signed before it is read.

I cannot give legal advice, value the house, or move money. I have kept the list, and I have told you plainly where I thought a proposal failed it. I was wrong once about item 5, and you corrected me.", "to": "C"}

function.name: finish
function.arguments:
{"report": "The family has moved from open conflict to a shared list of concerns and a plan of information-gathering, with no decision made on price.

Where things stand:

The will and the estate are still unknown. None of the three sisters knows who holds the will or who is the executor. They have each taken one enquiry: C is checking their dad's papers at home, A is contacting the solicitor and any will register, and B is contacting the bank and other financial institutions. All three accepted a two-week target for these enquiries, and all three were clear it is a target for gathering information, not a deadline for a decision.

The list of concerns, agreed by all three, covers nine items: finding and reading the will; establishing the estate's assets and debts; an independent valuation of the house before any discount is discussed; B speaking for herself; any discount coming only out of A's own share; the separate and still open question of whether there is a discount at all; target dates so an empty house does not drain the estate; written terms checked by a lawyer before signing; the work not falling on one sister alone; and no price or option agreed before the will and valuation are in hand.

The main shift is on the price question. A first asked to buy at a family discount, which C refused. A has now said a discount means she uses her own share toward the house and pays B and C for theirs, not that they accept less than their share is worth. C and B both said they would accept A buying at the full independent valuation in principle. So all three now agree no sister should receive less than her share is worth. The one open practical question is whether A and her husband can raise two thirds of the valuation.

I corrected myself once. I had said the discount question was settled when A offered to fund a discount from her own share. C rightly disagreed, and the list now separates the funding rule from the question of whether a discount happens at all.

Nothing has been signed and no money has moved. I gave no legal, tax, or mortgage advice, and I told the family each time that a lawyer and a lender are needed for those parts. The next real step is theirs: the three enquiries, then the will, then the valuation, and only then a price for A to test against the list."}
